query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Fully substituting the heavy Hf with additional Zr in the HfMoTaTiZr alloy will lower the overall density while preserving its single-phase solid solution and the solution-strengthening mechanism that underpins its high strength at both room and elevated temperatures (~1000 °C).
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a density of 10.21 g/cm³ and high mechanical strength at room temperature and elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Replace Hf entirely with an increased content of Zr to form a Hf-free (or Hf-reduced) alloy (e.g., an equiatomic or near-equiatomic variant such as ZrMoTaTiZr or MoTaTi2Zr) that retains the same overall phase characteristics.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing at room temperature and under elevated temperature conditions around 1000 °C, under compressive and/or tensile loads.
generation.structural_mediator: A single-phase disordered solid solution with similar lattice distortion arising from comparable atomic radii; the substitution maintains the beneficial solution strengthening effects.
generation.mechanism: Since Zr has a lower atomic mass than Hf but a similar atomic size and chemical behavior, replacing Hf with Zr reduces the alloy’s overall density while maintaining the lattice distortion and solid solution strengthening that secure high strength over a wide temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significant decrease in density relative to 10.21 g/cm³ with little to no compromise in yield strength and high-temperature performance when compared to the original as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy.
generation.baseline: The as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy’s density and mechanical properties (high strength and stability at room temperature and around 1000 °C).
generation.boundary: The alloy is expected to perform within the temperature range from room temperature to approximately 1000 °C under standard mechanical loading conditions; the phase stability and solid solution behavior must be maintained within this range.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding how the increased Zr content might subtly alter the lattice parameters and the exact magnitude of the solid solution strengthening effect. Detailed phase stability and microstructural analyses are required to ensure that no deleterious phases form that could compromise mechanical performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of alloys in which Hf is fully substituted by Zr (with appropriate adjustment of other element ratios to maintain overall equiatomic balance). Characterize the resulting alloys using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and electron microscopy (SEM/TEM) to confirm the retention of a single-phase solid solution. Measure the density using the Archimedes method and evaluate mechanical properties (yield strength, ductility, and high-temperature stability) through compressive/tensile tests at room temperature and at ~1000 °C.
measurements: Mechanical properties (yield strength, ductility, compressive/tensile strength) at room temperature and ~1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Zr-substituted alloy exhibits either a significant loss of mechanical strength (at room temperature or ~1000 °C) or the formation of additional phases indicating a loss of a stable single-phase solid solution, despite a reduced density compared to 10.21 g/cm³, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: There are some researches working on the addition of Al [,], Mo [], Ti [], V [], or Zr [], but few of them focus on the elevated-temperature mechanical performance and the overall effect of the constituent elements. To understand the elemental effect on mechanical properties, equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy is firstly designed as a base alloy by adding the high modulus refractory element Mo to HfNbTaTiZr. Then the subtraction method is used to analyze each elemental effect in the equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr. Thus, in this study, six alloys HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi are investigated and compared on their microstructure. Further, the compressive properties at room temperature and at elevated temperature are investigated. By comparing HfMoNbTaTiZr and HfNbTaTiZr, the influence of the addition of Mo can be understood. Likewise, the influence of the addition of Nb, Ta, Ti, or Zr can be articulated. In addition, promising compositions were found and further improved design is suggested. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solid solution strengthening effect will be discussed.

Our first attempt in research of HEAs was therefore related to HfNbTaTiZr refractory metal alloy []. Our research was inspired by Senkov [] and confirmed our expectations. Ingots produced by vacuum arc melting possessed single phase solid solution microstructure, with a high room temperature tensile strength and ductility. Some of the elements used in the HfNbTaTiZr alloy are very similar to each other with very similar chemical behaviour; Nb is chemically similar to Ta and Zr to Hf. Therefore a question has emerged whether it is necessary to use all of these elements in order to get random solid solution and good mechanical properties (high strength and sufficient ductility). The design of the present experiment was as follows. First, we reduced the original HfNbTaTiZr alloy system by removing Hf, which is almost identical to Zr from the chemical point of view, then we distracted Ta, which is very similar to Nb; thus getting NbTiZr alloy with equiatomic concentrations. Then we produced also other 3 element combinations containing Ti, namely TaTiZr and NbTaTi. Several theoretical models of solid-solution strengthening have been proposed to explain how different constituent elements affect room-temperature or elevated-temperature strength [,]. We previously designed a RHEA that exhibited higher elevated-temperature strength and discussed the effect of the constituent elements on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys by using the subtraction method []. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add elements such as Mo, which significantly interact with the other elements. For higher elevated-temperature strength, one should add the elements that possess a high melting point such as Mo, Nb, or Ta. For higher ductility, one should add more Nb. With Ti or Zr addition, both the elevated-temperature strength and the density decrease.
